title: Thévenin's Theorem: Any Linear Circuit Becomes One Source
topic: Thévenin's theorem — any linear two-terminal network can be replaced by an open-circuit voltage V_th in series with an equivalent resistance R_th; the load sees the same current and voltage either way

beats.narration: A messy box of sources and resistors drives a load — how can we treat the whole thing as one battery?

elements.content: A circuit with two terminals — what does the load really see?

beats.narration: Here is the network — two sources, three resistors, and a load on the right. The load sees a voltage at its terminals and a current through it.

elements.content: Two-source three-resistor network: V1 in series with R1 on top branch, V2 in series with R2 on bottom branch, R3 across the terminal pair, load R_L to the right
Terminal labels a and b at the load junction
I_L current arrow flowing into the load
from the load's perspective, the rest is a black box

beats.narration: Disconnect the load. The voltage that appears across the open terminals is V Thevenin — the open-circuit voltage of the network.

elements.content: Same network but load R_L slides away to the right — terminals a-b now open
Voltmeter symbol across the open terminals reading V_th

beats.narration: Now zero the independent sources — every voltage source becomes a wire. The resistance you see looking back into the terminals is R Thevenin.

elements.content: Same network with V1 and V2 replaced by short wires; resistor network simplifies
Ohmmeter symbol across terminals reading R_th

beats.narration: Put V Thevenin in series with R Thevenin, reconnect the load, and the current is identical. The load can't tell the difference.

elements.content: Two stacked circuits — top: original messy network with load and charge dots flowing through R_L; bottom: V_th source + R_th resistor + load with the same flow rate
Both ammeters read the same I_L
